questions.question: Q1. Why does the WLF equation apply only above T_g and not below it?

answers.a: Because the material becomes conductive below T_g and WLF applies only to insulators.
answers.b: Because below T_g the chains are frozen and segmental motion is absent, making the relaxation time effectively infinite.
answers.c: Because below T_g the material is liquid and WLF only applies to solids.
answers.d: Because the WLF constants change sign below T_g.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Conductivity is not the reason; WLF is about molecular mobility.
explanations.b: Correct — Below T_g the glassy state locks the chains; there is no dynamic relaxation, so the WLF model breaks down.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Below T_g the material is solid (glassy), not liquid.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The constants C_1 and C_2 do not change; the model simply does not apply in the frozen regime.

questions.question: Q2. A PU-SMP (T_g = 45°C, X_c = 0.85) is programmed at 70°C under 5 MPa stress with E_rubbery = 15 MPa. What is the approximate strain fixity ratio?

explanations.a: Correct — R_f = 0.85 × [1 - exp(-1.67)] ≈ 0.85 × 0.81 ≈ 69%, closest to 75% among the options.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Closer, but the saturation formula with (T_prog - T_g)/15 = 25/15 = 1.67 gives higher fixity.
explanations.c: Incorrect — This underestimates the fixity at a 25°C margin above T_g.
explanations.d: Incorrect — This assumes full saturation, which requires a much larger temperature margin.

questions.question: Q3. In the recovery kinetics sub-calculator, why does free recovery (no external load) reach ε_recovered = 0 but constrained recovery stops at a finite ε_eq > 0?

answers.a: Free recovery is faster than constrained recovery.
answers.b: Free recovery is limited by friction between chains.
answers.c: In free recovery the material can shrink indefinitely; under a load the rubbery modulus produces a resisting stress that balances the programmed strain.
answers.d: Constrained recovery requires lower temperatures to activate.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Both follow the same exponential law, but reach different endpoints.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Friction slows relaxation but does not set the endpoint.
explanations.c: Correct — Free recovery has no opposing force (ε_eq = 0), so the material relaxes completely. Under constraint, the recovered material generates a restoring stress (σ = E_rubbery × ε_eq / 100) that eventually balances the driving force.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Temperature activates both in the same way; the boundary condition determines the endpoint.

questions.question: Q4. The DSC (Differential Scanning Calorimetry) heat capacity model in Sub-Calc A uses a smooth step function centered at T_g. Why is this smooth transition physically more realistic than a sharp step?

answers.a: Because the smooth step better models the heterogeneous distribution of relaxation times near T_g in a real polymer.
answers.b: Because polymers are not ideal materials and transitions are gradual.
answers.d: Because the material's density changes smoothly near T_g.

explanations.a: Incorrect — While true, the main reason is material non-ideality.
explanations.b: Correct — Real polymers do not exhibit infinitely sharp transitions; the smooth sigmoidal step centered at T_g (with width w = 8) captures the actual breadth of the glass transition.
explanations.c: Incorrect — This is a minor computational consideration, not the physical reason.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Density change is not the primary reason; it is the breadth of the relaxation spectrum.

questions.question: Q5. In the multi-shape (phase-separated) blend sub-calculator, why does the intermediate shelf exist between T_g1 and T_g2?

answers.a: The material undergoes a chemical reaction that suspends strain recovery.
answers.b: The shelf is an artifact of the simulator and does not occur in real materials.
answers.c: The material crystallizes at the intermediate temperature.
answers.d: The soft phase (PU) has relaxed its strain at T_g1, but the hard phase (PMMA) remains glassy and its entropic restoring force is blocked until T_g2.

explanations.a: Incorrect — No chemical reaction occurs; it is purely a mechanical effect.
explanations.b: Incorrect — The plateau is real and directly results from the two-phase morphology.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Crystallization does not govern the plateau.
explanations.d: Correct — At T_g1 the soft PU domains soften and release their programmed strain, but the hard PMMA phase remains glassy (E_eff ~ 7.5 MPa) and does not soften until T_g2, creating a recovery plateau.

questions.question: Q6. The Fox equation combines two T_g values to predict a blend's single glass transition. What does this assume about the blend morphology?

answers.a: That the two components are completely miscible (form a single homogeneous phase).
answers.b: That the two components form separate phases and do not interact.
answers.c: That the blend will crystallize at a predictable rate.
answers.d: That the interface between components is chemically bonded.

explanations.a: Correct — The Fox equation applies to miscible blends where the two polymers form a single, homogeneous phase with one averaged T_g.
explanations.b: Incorrect — When phases are separate (immiscible), the two T_g values appear as distinct recovery steps, not a single T_g.
explanations.c: Incorrect — The Fox equation does not predict crystallization.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Chemical bonding is not a requirement for the Fox equation to apply.

questions.question: Q7. In Sub-Calc E (thermodynamic efficiency), why does the overall efficiency η remain low (1-5%) even though the stored elastic energy can be substantial?

answers.a: Because most of the material dissipates energy as heat through internal friction.
answers.b: Because the load is too heavy for the material to lift.
answers.c: Because the sensible heat capacity (m·C_p·ΔT) required to raise the specimen's temperature dwarfs the elastic energy available, so most input heat goes into temperature rise rather than doing work.
answers.d: Because the material loses its shape memory after one cycle.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Internal friction contributes to losses, but it is not the dominant factor.
explanations.b: Incorrect — The load and recovery stress are specified; the efficiency problem is thermodynamic, not mechanical.
explanations.c: Correct — Since η = W/Q and Q includes both temperature rise (m·C_p·ΔT ≫ U_stored) and the elastic energy, the vast majority of input heat raises the bulk temperature, leaving only a small fraction for mechanical work.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The material retains its memory across cycles; degradation is not the issue.

questions.question: Q8. How does the crystallinity limit X_c in the strain fixity formula explain why different materials achieve different maximum R_f values?

answers.a: Higher X_c means the material melts at a lower temperature.
answers.b: X_c determines the mechanical strength of the permanent netpoints.
answers.c: X_c is the cooling rate required to lock the temporary shape.
answers.d: X_c represents the fraction of polymer chains that can be permanently locked by netpoints; materials with higher X_c can fix more strain before reaching saturation.

explanations.a: Incorrect — X_c is not a melting property.
explanations.b: Incorrect — X_c modulates fixity, not the strength of individual netpoints.
explanations.c: Incorrect — X_c is not a rate parameter.
explanations.d: Correct — The saturating exponential R_f = X_c·[1-exp(-(T_prog-T_g)/15)] is capped by X_c (PU=0.85, PLA=0.70, PMMA=0.60), reflecting each material's ability to lock strain via crystalline and cross-linked regions.

questions.question: Q9. In the WLF shift factor calculation, log(a_T) becomes increasingly negative as T rises well above T_g. What is the physical meaning of a very large a_T (say, 1000)?

answers.a: The material has become too stiff to deform.
answers.b: The relaxation time at T is 1000 times shorter than at T_g, meaning the polymer is highly fluid and chains relax very rapidly.
answers.c: The relaxation time at T is 1000 times longer than at T_g.
answers.d: The material has undergone a phase transition to a liquid.

explanations.a: Incorrect — High a_T indicates faster relaxation, not stiffening.
explanations.b: Correct — a_T = τ(T) / τ(T_g); if a_T = 1000, then τ(T) is 1/1000 of τ(T_g), indicating much faster chain dynamics at the higher temperature.
explanations.c: Incorrect — a_T is a ratio of relaxation times; large a_T means faster, not slower, relaxation.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The polymer may be more fluid, but it remains solid; a phase transition is not guaranteed.

questions.question: Q10. Consider a biomedical implant using PU-SMP with a programmed strain ε_u = 1.0 (100%), volume V = 10 cm³, mass m = 11 g, ρ = 1.1 g/cm³, C_p = 1.6 J/g°C. Approximately how much heat (in joules) is needed to raise it from 20°C to 45°C?

explanations.a: Correct — Q = m·C_p·ΔT = 11 g × 1.6 J/(g·°C) × 25°C = 440 J. This bulk sensible heat dwarfs the stored elastic energy (a few tens of joules), illustrating why efficiency is low.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Close, but under-estimates the actual value.
explanations.c: Incorrect — This assumes ΔT = 2°C or half the mass.
explanations.d: Incorrect — This would require either double the mass or double the temperature rise.
